utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you too. Shall we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be continuing your testimony today, and before we do that, please I'd like you to repeat your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and Mr. Ackerman may proceed with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic. How are you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to just remind you of what we talked about yesterday, how it will be much easier and much quicker if you can do your best to answer the question that I ask you and not some other answer that you might want to give. I want to you have back -- I guess it's not back. I want you to have a document, DB113. I don't know if you've ever seen this document before. Do you know that after foreign journalists had visited Omarska, that the CSB in Banja Luka set up a commission to investigate Omarska and what was going on there. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you have before you is a report that Simo Drljaca wrote to explain to the CSB in Banja Luka what had been going on in the Prijedor municipality with regard to Omarska. Have you seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Perhaps it was shown to me during one of my previous testimonies but I cannot confirm that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look through it, I think you might conclude that what Drljaca was doing here was trying to cover up what had been done in Prijedor and at Omarska, and I don't know if you've had a chance to look at it enough that you could give me your feelings about that. Can you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I would get enough time to read it, then I could give you a complete opinion. This way is hard for me to say just at first glance what the objective was of Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. Let's just look at some parts of it. On the first page, let me see if I can help you find it, it's in the second paragraph, about halfway down, Drljaca reports to Banja Luka, "The representatives of civilian organs of authority and SDS activists have undertaken a series of activities throughout the municipality and have established numerous contacts with elected representatives of the Muslim and Croatian peoples with a view to achieving agreement on the peaceful and civilised disarming of citizens and the acceptance of the established government while guaranteeing all civic, national, and religious rights and freedoms to all loyal citizens of the Serbian Republic." Was it your observation that that was true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not true in my opinion, and according to my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So at least for that part, you could, I think, agree with me that Drljaca was seeking to mislead the authorities in Banja Luka about what was going on in Prijedor, at least to that extent?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that what was read did not match the actual situation and now what Simo Drljaca's objective was is a different matter. That is his own affair. That may be part of his agreement with senior authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at the next page, about halfway -- it's the next page in English, at least. It's about halfway through -- it's the same paragraph you were reading from just further down, language starts with, "At the beginning of May." Drljaca says, "At the beginning of May, extremists provoked the first incident in the village of Hambarine when they stopped a group of soldiers without any reason. On that occasion, they resorted to using their weapons, killing three and seriously injuring two soldiers." Now, that part you know to be true, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this incident did occur. As for the number of persons who participated in it, I know about that from Serb sources, so I don't know about it from some independent source but I know what I heard from Serb sources through their radio links.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also know that this was the first incident in the Prijedor municipality involving what could be called shooting between military forces of one form or another?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the information from the Serb side, that was the first incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was, wasn't there, a very well organised operation going on in the Prijedor municipality to arm the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was very poorly organised, because it became more difficult to carry through mobilisation and to train the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at DB107, please. Tell the -- tell the Trial Chamber, if you can, what this document is, that you have in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the opportunity of seeing this during my last testimony, that's when it was shown to me. My personal opinion is that I doubt the authenticity of this document. It is some kind of minutes but first of all, there is the minutes of the 24th of October and then afterwards, the 6th of September, as if that were chronological and then again November. So there is not much logic in these minutes, and another thing, on one page, three times instead of saying 1991, it says 1992, and then it was corrected into 1991. So out of six dates, three are wrong and were subsequently corrected to the year when all of this took place. But what really confused me was this chronology so first the meeting in October was held, and after that, the meeting in September. What is mentioned here is the SDA, then some members of the party, and I was asked about this during my previous testimony, and I did give some opinion of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I know you did. Don't you think that if someone were trying to forge a document like this, that they probably would be a great deal more careful in making an effort to make it look authentic? It looks, does it not, like just the random notes of someone about what was going on in these meetings that were being held? Doesn't it look like that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that it was hardly likely for someone to write 1992 three times and then correct it into 1991, and all of this on a single sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at -- let's look at the first entry in this document. It says, "At the SDA meeting of 24 October, 1991, at the SDA meeting, the following were assigned to weapons duty." And then it lists people from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. various villages, Kozarac, Kenjar and Bahonjic; Trnopolje, Sead Sivac; Kozarusa, Tadzic; Brdo and Ljubija; Kadiric, Hopovac, Sikiric; and Puharska, Rufad Suljanovic. Did you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that they were assigned to weapons duty in these various localities?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. This is a larger number of people, and I would have certainly known had any of them had any specific duty and I know full well that some of them were not in the Territorial Defence at all. I know that Dr. Suljanovic did not have anything to do with anything related to this or was any kind of SDA meeting held during this period of time at which any kind of weapons were discussed. So this simply is not true. The date here is the 24th of October, 1991. It said 1992 and then it was corrected into 1991. If we believe this to be the correct date, then absolutely it was not possible to have weapons discussed at party level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at -- you know what Eso -- is Eso a name, E-S-O?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eso S. Very often the name Esad is abbreviated Eso, so this is a nickname that is frequently referred to. Then the congress in Sarajevo is mentioned so it's probably Dr. Eso Sadikovic, Dr. Esad Sadikovic. He was nominated as an independent candidate to be invited to the SDA congress in Sarajevo. That is indeed a fact and I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at the entry for 6 September of 1991. It says, "Recruits to stay within Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what the person who wrote this meant, but I do know what the discussions were at the time regarding the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you answered my question. You don't know. I want to ask you the same question about the next entry, "Records to be removed." Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The entry for 20 November, 1991, it says, "Against mobilisation, threaten with the UN and The Hague. Print announcement 300 copies." Do you have any idea what that's about?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall such things, let alone that somebody was issuing any threats related to The Hague in any way. I don't think that the notion of The Hague was not really very well known at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there was actually a peace conference that was held here in The Hague regarding what was going on in Yugoslavia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that a conference was held in Lisbon and that that was discussed very extensively. There was information coming in every day about the course of those negotiations and then also in Macedonia, Skoplje, Brioni, the interrepublican negotiations that were being held in all these places. Later on, when I testified before this Court, this paper was shown to me and there was this conference on Yugoslavia that was held in The Hague, as far as I can remember, but that was probably the beginning of this process of international negotiations, and in the public, it was not really that well known, not as well known as the following sessions. In this context, I don't know what it means to threaten someone by referring to a conference where everybody participating -- participated on a footing of equality. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next entry is 20 November, 1991, it says, "AD 6. A Izetbegovic that's probably Alija Izetbegovic's order to have the police force increase, although the Minister of the Interior requested that the reserve force be dissolved." Do you have any idea what that means?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything with certainty regarding this particular matter. I was not very well-versed. I know that the Territorial Defence was discussed but as for the police, I don't remember, because that really was not my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "The introduction of religious instruction and Muslim people's culture." Does that make any sense to you? Hadn't there been religious instruction and cultural matters before that date?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first part is logical. The parliament unanimously decided, that is to say the members of all ethnic groups, and all parties, that the legislation should make it possible to introduce religious instruction everywhere in all -- as regards all the religions but of course this would be an optional course, but as for the rest, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who this person, seems to be a person mentioned next, then, by the name of Camil Pezo. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Camil Pezo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is an entry there that reads, "On 23 September, 1991, appointed to the war Crisis Staff." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. That is the third paragraph, yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know about that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. On the 23rd of September, 1991, no Crisis Staff existed or was any such possibility mentioned, that is to have a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look on down, you see another entry, the same date, 23 September, 1991, "State of emergency, wartime conditions. Crisis Staff." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this period, it is quite illogical. I also see some names here that did not exist in the SDA. Underneath Crisis Staff it says Refik Krkic and Camil Pezo. There was no Refik Krkic in the SDA or any person that I know with such a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you now to look at a document DB-108?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm really seeking clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not lighting either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It definitely doesn't want the Prosecution to be heard today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this one working, the one in front? Or not. Not even?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do these things happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour maybe I'll just borrow the Defence. See if it's working. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think it is. You can use mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Rather than waste time I'll just -- it's really just clarification. Both the two documents that Mr. Ackerman has been asking about were asked about in the Stakic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first one at length. I understood that the agreement was that examination-in-chief would be done through the transcript being put in with a few additional questions but in fact what's happening it seems to me is that Mr. Ackerman's allowed to go through the whole thing all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, I'm sorry, my point is this: One of the problems when we agreed to this was we knew that Your Honour would only get a partly one sided view of it but if these matters have already been cross-examined to, unless there is a new matter, which is separate, a different matter, then Your Honour it's in the transcript already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it is in the transcript already but I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour with respect, you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I understand what you mean but how can I anticipate what Mr. Ackerman is going to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely right but if the point comes, I simply -- I'm asking for clarification. I don't want to keep leaping up and saying Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this is at page X of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For example this particular document, 107 that we have been just reviewing, the witness did say in Stakic that he gave it very little credibility, I mean he viewed it as a suspicious document. He's reiterated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again Your Honour with the previous one, the CSB report he went through that at some length, pages, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't in this instance. I mean he was only asked one question about one or rather three questions on three particular parts of -- from that report and that's it. So -- but I think -- I think it's very important and it's very useful that you have brought this up because I think Mr. Ackerman would tend to agree with most of what you're saying. At the same time, you need to appreciate that I am not Mr. Ackerman's mind. I don't know what he intends to ask and where he intends to lead the witness and what kind of information he requires. If it's -- he embarks on an exercise which is merely repetitive then I will stop him for sure. That's for sure but with regard to the previous document I don't think he was. With regard to this one, maybe he is, as you rightly say. But I think we will need to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt Your Honour but rather than waste time because as Mr. Ackerman is I'm anxious to try and get this witness through. I'm merry raising the matter for Your Honour's consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I appreciate that. That was on my mind actually but I have this problem not knowing exactly what to expect from the cross-examination at any time. It's -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll just respond to this extent only. There are huge parts of the cross-examination that was done in the Stakic case that I intend to rely on and not bring up at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I also --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page after page after page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also understand that it may well be your intention to try and discredit the witness. I don't know. But in that case, obviously you will need to go through parts of his previous testimony in detail but if that is the case. I don't think you're heading that way but -- yes, maybe we will get some enlightenment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I notice now that one of the witness's microphones has gone dark and I don't know...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we will attend to that first, make sure. It's on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are making progress. They are both on now. There we go. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. I think you should have before you now DB108. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I know you've also seen this document before. It was shown to you in the Stakic case. And was made an exhibit in that case. If you'll go to -- there is a number 3, miscellaneous, and a person by the name of Nagib, indicates that a person by the name of Nagib speaks. Do you know who Nagib is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What Nagib appears to say is that "A lot of our people carry out acts of provocation. Fazlic and Hasan Didin yesterday fired in order to provoke. The police should immediately take such people to the police station and disarm them." And then someone named Suljo says, "Such men should be disarmed, that Didin takes drugs and he was at the front. Izmet Dergic should be criticised. Sons who drive him around and hang out with him." Do you know who Suljo is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one. I know there was a Suljo in Kozarac, but now which Suljo is that escapes me. However, I know that when you started reading this, you added something that doesn't say here. It says Fazlic and Hasan Didin fired. The police should then bring in them and disarm them and you said that they fired in order to provoke. It does not say here, I'm looking at the original document, I'm looking at what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't say in the original document that they yesterday fired in order to provoke? That language is not there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't. The sentence ends with the word "fired."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So the translation apparently is wrong. If you'll look at a section that begins with the number 5 at the top of it, and the first -- it says it's a report from last night's meeting and mobility and elimination of faults or something like that. The first person that speaks is named Bahonja.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find it. Could you tell me where is it? You said number 5 at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to look at the B/C/S and see if I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's page 342. In this handwritten, printed, you have IT 94-1-A and then 342.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a 342 in the upper right-hand corner, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's the first three lines that you're being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The actual part I'm referring you to is where it's the third person down, Beco, Beco speaks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fourth person, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fourth person, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see Beco there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He says, "We have to know what is our position for tomorrow's meeting. I have nothing against a Serb going but you all know what this Dule did against the people of Kozarac. You, Hamdo, are fighting for your physical survival in Kozarac and at the same time pushing Dule for the negotiations." Now are they talking about a delegation that's going to go speak to the authorities in Prijedor and is the person they are talking about there Dusko Tadic or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure because there is no surname here. I know, however, that several Serbs took part in some negotiations and talks about problems at the time. Dule Tadic did live in Kozarac and it could be he.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know any other Serb who lived in Kozarac who had that nickname Dule?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you just go down a little bit further, you'll see a Kemo S speak. Do you know who Kemo S is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, you're previous question, if my -- if I remember correctly, there was a policeman who was also nicknamed Dule but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who Kemo S is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a Kemal or Kemo Fazlic in Kozarac so since I see here initial "F" it could be Kemal Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a Beco?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is that? Who is Beco?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin, secretary of the secretariat for national defence of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So Kemo S says, "Beco, the people of Kozarac will never forgive you if you drag them into war. Let Dule be a member of the negotiating team." In other words he's responding to what Beco said about Dule in that earlier part we read, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it looks like, within this context, but I can hardly speak about that because I do not remember attending any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you now go forward several pages, you should find another document that is headed at the top, "Meeting of Kozarac and Kozarusa local communes." It has the date 6-6-92 but I think -- I think we'll find it's actually May of 1992 and I think we'll discover that here in a moment. It would be 6 May of 1992, the date of that meeting. Do you know anything Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about this meeting that is set out in these minutes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific -- at that time there were several meetings. There were meetings of this kind or another almost daily, so that it is difficult for me to single out, to identify some of them. I did attend a certain number of them. However, not the -- I didn't attend a much larger number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who Ibro Kahrimanovic was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was somebody in Kozarac who was called Ibro Kahrimanovic. What he did, whether he held some office, what office, that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume you knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I saw his photograph, perhaps I would know it then, whether I knew him as it is, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's reported to have said in this meeting, "We do not want to wear any insignia. Inhabitants of Kozarusa are resentful of the fact that the president of the municipality and parties parade through the town. They should be solving problems in their own area of town. Inhabitants of Kozarac said that from then on, they would not let them go further than the Koncar factory." Do you know anything about what he's saying there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any Koncar factory. I know there was a fabrics, a textile factory or ready-made clothes. There was a sawmill. Whether this textile factory was -- whether it was called Koncar, no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look a little further -- so you don't know what the Koncar factory is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know and I don't know what this man meant when he said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look a little further, you'll see Hamdija speak. First, just above that, you'll see your own self, Sejmenovic, and Sejmenovic is reported to have said, "I can see two solutions. Insignia or no insignia on the police. However, a question of security is being raised. Who is going to protect them if we surrender our weapons? Many people would get killed if we choose to procrastinate we have to make all possible effort. I am against the idea that people are left unprotected. I would rather we tried to defend ourselves." That's what you said at that meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is what my opinion looked like. I think it was slightly different. Now whoever worded this, if the minutes, if this record is correct, and the person who took the minutes, of course, it is -- it depends on how he perceived it. The fact is that we were trying to provide for the security and obtain guarantees from the Serb side not to be attacked and to offer guarantees from our side that we would not provoke them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know who Osman was, don't you? Who speaks just shortly after you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several Osmans. I know there was one Osman in the police. There was one such man in the police. And I think he was a commander there but I'm not sure, and he was nicknamed Osma [phoen]. Whether it is he that we see here or somebody else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at what he says there, I think it's -- it will help you clear up the proposition that this is the person who was chief of police there in Kozarac. What he says was, "Many things will be clearer tomorrow. Banja Luka will make a decision. If they decide to introduce insignia, I will have to sacrifice my life for the Serbian state. The police wants the people to speak up." Do you know what he means when he says, "I will have to sacrifice my life for the Serbian state"?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look a little further along in the document, there is a person by the name of Pasic who speaks. Do you know who Pasic is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is Dr. Jusuf Pasic from Kozarac, because I don't know if there were any other Pasics in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Pasic says, according to this, "I agree with the comrades. We are occupied. The aggressor imposes its authority on us. We can either accept it until some better times or get into war." Do you recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. I cannot recall that, but I do know Dr. Pasic and I know that he came from the socialist democratic party. As far as I know, he held no office, either in the Territorial Defence or in any other local authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He talks about either accepting what it is, and that has to do with these insignia, I assume, accepting that or getting into war. And actually, preparations were being made at that time for the possibility of a war, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preparations were under way in so far as it was possible, but they were meant for the defence, to prevent the massacre of the population, such as we have already had the opportunity to see in the media in other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you'll look a little further now on, you'll come to a section headed, "8-5-1992." I take it that's 8 May of 1992. And at the top, it has a list of agenda items, I take it, 1, 2, and 3. Page 332, the top right-hand corner, it's page 332, I think. And you should see a section of that where Husein M speaks. I cannot find it in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 333 in the B/C/S version, page 333.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second half of bottom part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, near the bottom of page 333, the Judge has found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you find it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Husein M? No, no, I haven't. I haven't found it. No Husein M is mentioned here or I mean I can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 333 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Handwritten page 333.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I see it, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just take a minute and look at that and let me know when you -- I just want you to read that little section there of what's attributed to Husein M.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Husein M, "When we were talking about the municipality, it turned out --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can just read it to yourself. You don't have to read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it more or less, because some words I couldn't make out, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Basically what he seems to be talking about there are the negotiations that are going on in Lisbon regarding a possible settlement of the issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and indicating that Izetbegovic on behalf of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim people, may sign an agreement that provides for a Serbian canton in the Prijedor area, and he indicates that, "We will accept any decision made in Lisbon." And then in the last sentence says, "Try to arrange a meeting at any cost with Zupljanin or Radic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes, at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it that the Zupljanin and Radic that he'd be talking about are either -- are Stojan Zupljanin, the head of the CSB in Banja Luka, or Predrag Radic, who was the President of the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know why Husein M would be saying to arrange a meeting with them at any cost?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Hamdo Balic, who is mentioned in the text at the beginning of the page is a friend of Mr. Radic and Mr. Zupljanin's friend too, and he is a kind of an in-law of Mr. Kupresanin. I mean they were personal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. friends, and it was thought that Hamdija would be able to establish a good communication with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that would be communication regarding this issue of the insignia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything, all the matters that were discussed. We were really expecting a great deal from Mr. Balic and other people, other officials from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally the very last entry in this document, a person by the name of Bahonjic speaks. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bahonjic, I guess it is Islam Bahonjic from Kamicani. He was in the SDA. He was a councilman in the municipal assembly and as far as I can remember, he was involved with the Territorial Defence at a later stage when it was expanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he says, does he not, that "if the people from Kozarac want to surrender the weapons, let them do so. The people from Jakupovici will kill a few Serbs." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. This isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should be the very last entry in this document, if my translation is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he have 347?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. 338. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. It's a different place. And that's what he says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here. That's what's written down here, the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's in fact what happened in that location, Jakupovici, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They actually destroyed a Serb tank that was in a convoy, right, and killed a few Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know who was around the tanks and on the tanks. These were the military. And here reference is made to the actual people. But the army moved later. Now, this is another question. This is a -- this is the situation before the war. The nervousness, the tensions before the war. So on this date, there was a tank at the entrance into Kozarac and it was facing Kozarac. 20 metres from the first houses. Later on, it retreated. I think that these two things have nothing to do with each other. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about a different event. I think it was on the 24th of May, and I may be off a day or so, when a Serb convoy was travelling along the highway at Jakupovici. That convoy was attacked by Muslim forces, a tank was destroyed, Serb soldiers were killed. That was done on the orders of captain Cirkin. They were ordered to fire by Captain Cirkin. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know what the stand of Territorial Defence was. If the population is attacked, an attempt will be made to defend them. The only other news regarding the situation in Jakupovici and in other parts of Prijedor is something that we know about from Serb sources. I cannot trust them. It is up to the competent authorities to establish through appropriate proceedings what actually did happen. Physically, I was not present in Jakupovici, and I cannot give my view on that. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is you don't know? That's the simple answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Again we are going to be here a long time if you can't just give me a simple answer like, "I don't know," because all I asked you was if you knew about that. I don't think that required a speech, did it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at another document, DB109. Sir, I would like to move very quickly through this document so please try to help me do that. This is a document dated 26 April, 1992, appears to be another meeting of some sort, lists some of the people who we've already seen as participating in it, and if you look down after all the folks have spoken, there is a list of weapons, and just, for example, it says that there are seven zolja hand-held rocket launchers, two in "Kam," two in "Koz," two in "Kevlj," and one in Kozarac. Those are -- that -- those are places where they are contending that these weapons are located. And my only question is, do you know anything about this distribution of weapons that seems to be set out in this document?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Territorial Defence had this right and this was their right and responsibility. Before the war, and in case of threat of war, to deploy weapons, distribute weapons. And I know that these are symbolical amounts in relation to the Territorial Defence, that accounts for a population of some 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look, then, at a page that begins at the top, "Omer," this document seems to talk about weapons that have been procured and how much was spent in procuring them and other weapons that are in the process of being procured, and how much it's going to cost to get those, speaks of several rounds of ammunition, apparently in various locations. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. That is the third sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this document is dated 26 April, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the date the first page bears, but the other two sheets of paper do not bear any date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 26th of April, 1992, was a few days before the takeover of Prijedor by Serbs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this was 20 days after the Serb tank was placed at the entrance into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And before there was ever a takeover in Prijedor, the Muslim people were procuring arms and arming themselves in preparation for war, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals tried to provide for their safety in that way, but later on, it was all taken over by a legal institution. That is the Territorial Defence. As can be seen from these documents, people brought in what they had and the Territorial Defence distributed that and gave it to various formations, according to official regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to sort of the middle part of May. I'm through with that document -- the middle part of May of 1992. The time I want to really direct your attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I bumped it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The time I want to direct your attention to is probably the middle of May, the 17th, I think, of May, maybe. You have testified previously about a mass meeting that went on in Kozarac that you participated in. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember partly this big meeting at the elementary school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that followed by a day or two a meeting that had gone on in Prijedor where the military commanders there, Zeljaja and Arsic, basically issued an ultimatum to Kozarac regarding the surrender of weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Perhaps it was the other way around, that first there was this meeting in Prijedor, with the Serbs, and then afterwards, the one at the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I may have left the wrong impression with you. That's exactly what -- I think there was a meeting in Prijedor on around the 16th of May, and then the meeting at the school in Kozarac around the 17th. I believe that's been your prior testimony, although you've not ever been certain on those dates. Those have been your best guesses and that's what I'm referring to. That mass meeting at the elementary school in Kozarac, you spoke at that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that I did take part in this particular meeting, but I cannot remember specifically what I spoke about. Perhaps some general statements, namely people from the Territorial Defence and the police who were professionally well-versed were the ones who were really handling things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only question I asked was, you spoke at that meeting, didn't you? Just answer that.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, if you want to come back next week or some later time, you can keep answering questions the way you're answering them but I'm trying to ask you questions that you can answer just with yes or no. At that time, when that meeting was held, you were a leader, a representative, of the people, a member of parliament, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, representative of the municipality, and what we are talking about here are local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you had a position in that area that was such that people looked up to you, relied upon you in some ways, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for importance, I ranked 7th or 8th in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it was --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was quite a -- quite an experience for someone that was 28 years old at the time, to be put into a position of such responsibility and authority, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in Kozarac at that time, parliamentary activity was not necessary. I was a member of parliament and it is well known what a MP is supposed to do. So what we are discussing here are Territorial Defence, police, et cetera, and I'm not a person who was competent, as far as such matters are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether my question was not translated properly or what, but I'm going to move on. Isn't it the case that at that meeting, you opposed the surrender of arms?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can certainly confirm to this Honourable Trial Chamber is that I did not present any proposals of a collective body. I was very careful, because I'm not competent enough. So I only presented personal views. At that point in time, I did not have any high degree of authority in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question. The question was a very simple one. Were you asked by Mr. Ackerman whether at that particular meeting, not any other meeting, that particular meeting, whether it's true that you opposed the surrender of arms. Answer yes or no, please. Because otherwise, we will go on and on and on. No one is expecting you to justify or explain your conduct during those years. You're not on trial here. Someone else is on trial. So you didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I answered and I gave an explanation. In the future, I am not going to give these additional explanations. So I did not oppose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We saw just a moment ago the minutes from a meeting where you're reported to have said that you were opposed to the surrender of arms. Do you remember us looking at that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was before the meeting in Prijedor, sir, where the ultimatum was addressed. Now we are in a different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time you're in that different context in Kozarac that you're talking about, you had no way to communicate with the republic authorities in Sarajevo, and therefore no way for to you take any instructions from Sarajevo, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I could not establish any contact with the authorities in Sarajevo. Even if I could have, that had not been my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when I speak of you in this context, I'm talking about the folks that were in that meeting trying to solve this problem, having no way to take instructions from Sarajevo, no way to contact Sarajevo. That group there in Kozarac at that time was effectively on their own, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly there were some radio links, but I don't know anything about that. The secretary of national defence, Mr. Medunjanin could have or should have established contact. Now, whether there were such contacts or not, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you basically found yourself in a position where you really had two options, you could become part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or reject that and try to remain a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, and that's really the dilemma that you were faced with at that point, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me read an answer you gave. This I think was in the Keraterm case, 14 July, 1998, page 649, what you told the Trial Chamber on that date was the following --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just for the correction for the transcript, it's actually the Kovacevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. You're exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 649 what you said was this: "We had two options, either to stop, cease being Bosnia-Herzegovina, and agree to enter the newly created Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, or to remain Bosnia and Herzegovina and the people decided to remain in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the decision reached at that meeting." That's what you said then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, but I was warned all the time, as I was today, that I should give only partial answers. We were threatened by slaughter, genocide. We had this experience. We saw it on television. And now you are talking about some kind of two formal options, to espouse one policy or the other. It was a question of trusting the Serb side. Nobody could have trusted them because in other municipalities, they had done something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've had an opportunity to listen to tapes of your prior testimonies before coming to testify in this case, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Only Stakic. He wasn't given any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wish there was a way I could give you this transcript, sir, and have you read it this evening but that can't happen, but I would challenge you to find in it some place where you were ordered by the Trial Chamber to give only partial answers, as you just said. If I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At that meeting, at that time, that we have been talking about, that you said you were left with two choices, two options, to put it a little more simply, the -- the options you had were to join them or fight them, and you chose to fight them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We decided to defend ourselves. If I can say "we" on behalf of all, all citizens, that is. If we are attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you told the Chamber in the Stakic case, and this would be at page 4553, referring to this early period of 1992, you said, "We were trying to find the best possible solution, the most intelligent solution, to get out of that situation, not to give them any pretext for any actions for the attack." That's what you told the Trial Chamber in Stakic just recently, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in fact, what you actually did was to choose not to turn in your weapons, to choose not to adopt the insignia of the new Serbian Republic, but to challenge and fight, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces were not challenged to fight. They established a para state and a paramilitary. They were not challenged. Whatever we did, they had well-developed plans and that's what they would have done, just like they did in the neighbouring municipality of Bosanski Novi where there was no Territorial Defence, no organisation whatsoever, where the people accepted insignia, handed over weapons, and they ended up the same way we did. And all of this happened before the events in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, don't you know that the police in Kozarac were engaging in repeated provocative actions by stopping and disarming Serb soldiers in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of any kind of repeated provocations. I simply do not believe that some kind of repeated provocative actions were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that the Kozarac police were frequently stopping and disarming Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that certainly doesn't fit in with an effort to find the best possible solution and not to give them any pretext for any actions for the attack, does it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what you mentioned, the frequent disarming of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any frequent disarming of soldiers. I simply don't believe it. I reject that. I don't know about that quite simply. I allow for the possibility of say some isolated incident that I had not heard about. Of course this is in contrast to the attempts made not to provoke incidents but also, the army sent its soldiers to provoke incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is it you're writing down over there? I notice you writing stuff. What are you writing?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can take a look, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't want to look at them. They are your private notes. I have no business looking at them. I'd just like to know what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm writing down some questions, because you often go back to previously put questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's what I'm writing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we take a break now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour may I just mention something before Mr. Ackerman continues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's this: Your Honour may recall that Mr. Sejmenovic gave an answer when he was being cross-examined about the Kovacevic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To the effect -- I'll just read it: That he said, "that's what I said because I was warned all the time as I was today that I should only give partial answers." And Mr. Ackerman said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That he would love to challenge him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Ackerman didn't want to take an unfair point and in fact we had a quick look at the Kovacevic transcript and we found on page 691, Defence counsel saying to him, "I asked you a very simple -- a simple question and if you can answer with very short answers," and then at page 651, it was put to him, "Your Honour if I may instruct the witness to just answer yes or no," and I'll follow up very quickly so I think everybody, and it's no criticism I'm sure of Mr. Ackerman but I think you can virtually say in every trial every witness is warned to try and control the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine because having lived this trial for almost a year now I realise that one of the biggest problems is precisely loquacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's common to all the trials and all the Trial Chambers that because we appreciate that witnesses want to give lengthy explanations that they are told to cut them off. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, I thank you, Ms. Korner, for your observations. Mr. Ackerman. Please remind the witness to answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will. I'll do my best. And with regard to what Ms. Korner just said I think that is not the same thing as being told to give partial answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want the witness to give full answers but sometimes a full answer is a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Sejmenovic, let's try to keep your answers as short as possible because I really would like to finish with you and -- by tomorrow. And I can. I can finish my questions?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only question I have is whether you can finish your answers or not. I want to talk to you for a little while about the actual battle that went on in Kozarac, part of which I think you were able to observe. And I'd like you to -- I want to refer you to something you said in the Stakic case about what you were observing. I'm on page 4683. You said, "The third night they burned the villages," and you were referring to a map so some of this doesn't make sense without the map but you say, "The infantry walked into the village from here and around 10.00 in the evening, they reached this part of Kozarac. And from this position that I'm pointing at now," that you were showing the Court where you were, you said, "We could see the soldiers run by the houses and we could see people trying to escape." Now, this time, when you use "we" are you referring -- are you including yourself in that? Did you see the soldiers run by the houses? And did you see people trying to escape?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the people and among other things, you could also see the silhouettes because the houses were lit by burning fires so that you could see the outline of persons running past them so that I also watched those scenes from a distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is a very simple one. Were you part of that group or is it indirect information that you're giving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've just drawn your attention to this problem, and you just fall into it again and again and again. Mr. Ackerman, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How far were you away from Kozarac at that point?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a definite answer but it was close to half a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at DB113 again. If you look on page 3 in the B/C/S version, sir, you find the second paragraph which begins with the words, "U toku." Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This again is that report written by Simo Drljaca that we were referring to a little bit earlier. It says, "During the fighting the army left a free corridor for all citizens who want to take shelter and flee from the zone of armed conflict. That's to say for all those who did not want to take part in an armed struggle against the army of the Serbian Republic. The army organised shelter for such citizens in the village of Trnopolje in the elementary school, the social centre, warehouse and neighbouring houses to ensure their safety. This is how the open reception centre of Trnopolje was established and it continues to operate to this day." True?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What's not true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of the sentence that you've just read out are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell me what's not true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take it one sentence after the other. First sentence, I am going to reed it to you myself. "During the fighting the army left a free corridor for all citizens who wanted to take shelter and flee from the zone of armed conflict that is to say for all those who did not want to take part in an armed struggle against the army of the Serbian Republic." Do you agree that during the fighting the army left such a free corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next. "The army organised shelter for such citizens in the village of Trnopolje in the elementary school, the social centre, warehouse and neighbouring houses to ensure their safety." Do you agree with this? With this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with this statement either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have the last sentence. "This is how the open reception centre of Trnopolje was established and it continues to operate to this day." Do you agree that the open reception centre of Trnopolje was established the way it is mentioned here? And that it was still in operation -- operating along those lines when this report came out? That is roughly, I would say, in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not the way how this reception centre came into being, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you've got your answer, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next sentence after the last one that we just read says this, "The centre has no barbed wire fence." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true. There was barbed wire in a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the entire centre was not surrounded by a barbed wire fence, was it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the entire centre. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a little further along, "The army secures the centre from attacks by extremists." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were troops in and around the centre. What they did, I do not know and I cannot answer that question. I mean I don't know whether they were involved in security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next sentence, "The number of citizens staying there varies because those who wish to can leave the centre at any time since there is a railway station located right by it." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it true that people were permitted to leave the centre if they had some place to go where they could stay safely?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subject to the authorisation of the Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It goes on, a little later to say, "The centre has a clinic with a medical team on duty round the clock equipped to extend basic medical care." Do you know if that was true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a medical team, but I do not think they were properly equipped and they -- there were no conditions there to extend health care apart from perhaps some basic interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you actually spent sometime at Trnopolje, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you entered that facility on your own. Nobody arrested you and took you there.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber how you were able to enter that facility.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crawling, at night-time. I crawled over the distance across fields, as we call them. I crawled through a channel, and sometime before the day break, I crawled under the barbed wire and joined the multitude of people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you mentioned in your testimonies or statement or something that you had seen some machine-gun nests, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to you look at a map. It's 1147.4. What you see there, sir, is a map represented to be a map of Trnopolje that was drawn by another witness here. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke about a machine-gun nest that was in the balcony of Hamdo's house. Can you show us on this map where Hamdo's house was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is that Hamdo's house that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where is the balcony of that house, where you saw the machine-gun nest?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facing -- the balcony faces in this direction. From here you can see the balcony directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Where is -- you also said there was a barn that had a machine-gun nest in it. Where is that? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's here in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was open here and faced the meadows in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so the machine-gun nest would be facing to the left of the barn? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Left if we look from here, and if we are facing the camp. So here in this part, and this is not really the barn. It is a covered facility but has no walls, and it serves to park vehicles. So it was in this part here, and I crawled through a channel which is here. I'm showing you the direction and which ran between two plots of land.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the transcript is not really going to show the things you were pointing at. Let's see if we can describe it for the transcript. To the left of some language that looks like it says, in your language, "Fudbalsko igraliste" or something like that. I think that's football field, football pitch. It's Hamdo's house is just right there to the left of that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we are looking from the Trnopolje-Prijedor road. If we are standing here, yes, we can see the football pitch and then the -- and then Hamdo's house is to the left. If we are on the other side, then it would be on our right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. Referring for the record referring to the sketch, the witness has pointed as being Hamdo's house the building that appears at 9.00 to the other building which is indicated as the skola.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour it may help, it's up to Mr. Ackerman, that we found a photograph which shows the house and that may help him. It's up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm happy with what we are doing. I just don't want the witness making marks on the Prosecutor's exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not. As regards the barn, the witness indicated the block of buildings at 12.00 of the other building referred to as skola.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's Exhibit P1128.1 if that can be shown to him. I think it's probably clearer on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at the photograph and just see what it shows. In the meantime, maybe the usher could make a copy of this exhibit so that I could have a separate copy that he could actually put a mark on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. You could have a photocopy of this document and it becomes a new document, a Defence document, and he can mark as much as he likes on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have in front of you now a photograph. Can you make a copy of that? You have in front of you now a photograph and where is -- where is Hamdo's house? Can you point to it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm pointing at it right now. And this is the balcony that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what -- and then you see the football pitch that's over there. You can see it fairly clearly, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can't see in this photograph the other building, though, that was a -- described as a barn, can you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it's in this direction where I'm pointing right now. So next to this meadow, in the extension of the school in this direction, there are several houses, then a road, and then again two or three houses and that is where this barn that we talked about is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Hamdo's house that you pointed to, this photograph is an exhibit, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's Exhibit P1128.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In P1128.1, the structure you pointed to is Hamdo's house is kind of a cream coloured, looks like a red roofed structure that sits at the other end of the football pitch from the school building, the white school building that sits there in front and it appears to have about three openings in the end that faces us in the photograph. Does that describe the building you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, yes. Hamdo's house has the ground floor and a loft from which you gain access to the terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In a moment we will have that other exhibit back and I'll ask you to mark the two places on it so there will be no question about it but let me ask you some other questions while we are waiting. Isn't it the case that the guards that were located around the camp were there to keep unauthorized persons from entering Trnopolje and not to keep persons there inside it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if they had wanted to keep people inside Trnopolje, don't you think they would have fenced them in?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a wire fence in parts, and in other places, where there were no wire fences, there were machine-gun nests. I heard from some people that there were some other machine-gun nests but I did not see them and they would be in this direction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you were able to go in and out, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, it was at night and crawling that I got there, towards the morning, and crawled under and joined the throng and that is how I left too and that is once again at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's try it again. You were able to go in and out, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really go -- get in and out. Had I been able to do that I would have taken the road rather than crawl.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You weren't shot at, were you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did not -- they did not see me get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You have this document, the map, and let's mark it as DB114. And what I'd like you to do is, the house you identified as Hamdo's house, could you just take a pen and just put the letters "HAM" on that house, just write them right on it or next to it or however you want to do it. Okay for the record you have written "HAM"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He can finish it he can write "Hamdo" I mean for just two letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead, write "Hamdo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness speaks English he can also write "Hamdo's house."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've written "Hamdo" above what was Hamdo's house. Now you're going to write the whole thing, "Hamdo's house." Very good. And that's written above the structure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Sejmenovic you could initial that, please. Put your initials against what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now go over to the barn and write the word "barn" there and put your initials?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really pinpoint the place where it was because I think that this is -- this sketch is not very accurate but I can tell you approximately where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For the record you've written what, what did you write and put in parenthesis there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote "kolara" and underneath, garage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please write "barn" because that's what we are interested in having indicated on that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right. You got it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've now written barn there also and you drew a line with an arrow on the end of it showing approximately where you believe that was located, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to have this document marked DB114.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I offer it in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm through with that now. We were -- we were in the midst of discussing my contention that the guards there were there to keep unauthorized persons out rather than to keep the people there in. There came a point when you came back to Trnopolje the second time, when you were advised to surrender, didn't there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
