utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were advised to do that by a person named Adem Trnjanin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not advise. He beseeched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's fine with me. And what he told you, and I'm referring now to your testimony in case IT-97-24-T, and I'm on page 699, what he told you was that this fellow Slavko, who was the head of the guards there, he told you that Slavko was only interested in how you entered the camp because Slavko was the head of the guards at the camp and he was only interested in how you were able to enter the camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Adem said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not interested in how you managed to get out but how you managed to get in, as if what Slavko, the head of guards, was interested in was how people were able to penetrate his efforts to keep people from getting into the camp unauthorized, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, when you were discussing the food situation at Trnopolje, you said, and it's page 4735, "They succeeded in obtaining an approval from the command of the camp for some people to be issued with a permit to go to their own homes and bring back flour so they could cook in the camp." That's true, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the reason they needed to be issued a permit was so that they could safely pass through checkpoints outside the camp in going back and forth to their homes?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the real reason was. They were probably keeping records as to who was leaving, who was leaving the camp from amongst the persons who had been in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if the -- I'm going to talk about Omarska for a moment now. Do you know if that facility was placed under the supervision of the army?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know formally under whose supervision it was. I know that Serb soldiers in uniform were there, as well as a few policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that report of Drljaca that we've been referring to periodically in your testimony, he said at one point that the police were entrusted with the task of providing direct physical security while the army provided in-depth security in the form of two circles and by laying mines along the potential routes of escape by prisoners. Do you know whether or not that's a true account?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. What I know is what I saw in the camp. I saw three types of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw blue police uniforms. As a matter of fact three persons with such uniforms, the kind we saw before the war. Then I saw for the most part ordinary soldiers' uniforms and I saw a few uniforms of special -- of the special police that I had seen a few days earlier at the prison in Prijedor. That is camouflage with a slightly purple hue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the purple uniforms were? Do you know what they represented?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think that's the special police but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I take it if I were to ask you about the numbers of people who passed through Omarska and the numbers that were transferred out of there to Trnopolje and Manjaca and things like that, you wouldn't really know about that. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm certain you recall the day that you were taken to Omarska, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I remember the approximate period. I never managed to remember the exact date, but I think it was the beginning of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm really asking you is whatever date it was, you certainly remember that day, remember what happened that day, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Do you mean do I remember which day in the week it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I realise that you're not understanding. What you are being asked, what you're being told is this: We understand that you do not remember the exact date when you were taken to Omarska, but Mr. Ackerman is suggesting to you that certainly you do remember the events of that day, of that particular day, and this is, I suppose what he is going to ask you about. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were first taken to the building known as the white house, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were beaten in the white house, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were in a room?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there was no other detainee in that room. You were the only detainee in there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And people were coming in and beating you and then leaving and then another person would come in and beat you and leave, and I think there were somewhere around five or seven people who actually came in there and beat you, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly how many there were but there were a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the first person that came in to beat you was a civilian. He was not military or police, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was a Muslim, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, I found out that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And sometime in that process, you were actually on the floor and you were kicked in the nose and the face so in your words, you were just completely bloody, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about when it was -- I know you don't know the exact date, but can you tell us about when it was that you went to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already stated that it was in the beginning of August. He couldn't remember the day -- the exact date but roughly he said it was the beginning of August, or at least he's got that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you there when there was a delegation that came to visit Omarska from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean Mr. Kupresanin, I was there on the spot. This was a few days later, in relation to what happened at the "white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, was that when Kupresanin came and rescued you and took you from there? Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came and he took me out of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you answered my question just a moment ago, that's the event you were referring to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from some camp inmates that there were other delegations coming in but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Your best guess is that it was right around the beginning of August when you were taken there and when you were beaten so severely over there at the white house, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the beginning of August. Perhaps it might have been the end of July, but I'm convinced that it had to be the beginning of August. Sometime around the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were interviewed by television there in Omarska and we saw a clip of that yesterday. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know that that was on the 5th of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. I beg your pardon. If this was on the 5th of August, then what we have been discussing now might have been towards the very end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I spent a short time in Omarska, perhaps between seven and nine days. That was my feeling any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to do is have the video director play just that part of the tape where you were interviewed, but this time with translation so we can hear what it was you were saying and look again at you in that process. So we can do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the video readily available for the technicians? Do they have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's all cued up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I want to make sure that the interpreters have understood that we need a running interpretation of what Mr. Sejmenovic says during -- in the course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I met with the interpreters during the break and pointed out the portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right, Mr. Ackerman. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've taken care of all of this, Your Honour. I'm a very efficient lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure that you were up to your usual high standard.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] They were interested in meeting prisoner Mevludin Sejmenovic member of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and SDA activist in the area. Question: We have heard that you were one of the rare inhabitants of this reception centre here that came to Omarska on his own. Answer: Yes, precisely. Question: Can you explain why you did that, how come you came here? Answer: I came here waiting and hiding around for a while. I waited for all the prime actors in these horrendous events to be captured, for the truth to be established, about what had happened, about the people that had done all that evil so that my efforts and work, as well as the statements I will give can be appreciated. Question: When you say capture who do you have in mind, who was responsible for all the horrors that took place in this area? Answer: I'm primarily referring to the party leader for Bosnian Krajina, Redjo Mucic [phoen] and chairman of the party branch in Prijedor, Mirzo Mucic [phoen] and member of the party executive council for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would also like to add all the men working in the party and organising these war-related activities. Question: Your fellow colleagues in this centre do they know about your opinion? Do they know about your views concerning the evil that befell the Muslim people? Answer: I have spoken about that on two occasions when we had discussions here in an interview for TV Krajina as well. I've made my statement and addressed a message to my people concerning this whole situation. I am now personally witnessing it in Bosanska Krajina in Prijedor. Not through a telescope, the way it is being watched by those who concocted all this evil. Question: I don't know whether you are aware of the fact that some foreign reporters mostly from Great Britain have also come to visit the centre. The reason for this visit is that over the past few days the international media have been claiming that in Republika Srpska, that is in the territory where you are now there are concentration camps for Muslims and Croats. Since you are in this particular centre and you came here of your own free will, as you said, could you tell these foreign reporters what the truth is? Do you know what a concentration camp is? Is this a concentration camp or is it a reception centre? What could you say to them? Answer: Well, I could say to them that it is the war operations that caused such effects that it became necessary for people to be grouped, both for reasons of safety and for mere survival in the final instance. This centre does not have the characteristics of a concentration camp, it's not the way the political propaganda has been putting it and I think that they have managed to see that for themselves today. Question: Just one more question. Before the flames of war actually started here, were there any among the Muslim people living in the area that were preparing for war? Answer: Over the past few months, those arms were talked about in every day conversations among ordinary people, let alone political parties, including the SDA. In fact, there was a great degree of fear and insecurity and people were looking for some kind of support, at least by talking about personal safety. However, it is now definitely clear that the political oligarchies were involved in very murky affairs, operating behind the back of the party members and the ordinary people. Their goal was to make the people fight for their private or individual interests without taking into account the real effects that could stem from such actions. I do not know. Perhaps it was even intentional. Since even foreigners have now come to the conclusion that this war has all the characteristics of a religious war, have you heard about some Muslim priests, hodzas, Imams, that had special hunting rifles, American-made, prepared even before the war? Answer: As for weapons and the process of procuring weapons, I really know very little about this. But ordinary people talked about this and there is evidence that a number of people have been involved, a number of priests were involved, in armed smuggling or some other form of weapon procurement. I only know that by doing so, they breached both the norms and the rules of the religion they preach as well as human moral norms, so they too have certain merits quote unquote, for all this evil that befell all the peoples living here."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I know that you've seen that clip a number of times and I first want to tell you that it is not my intention to challenge you with regard to that being the truth. I'm not going to do that. But I do have some questions I want to ask you about it. And the first one is that I would like to know if before that date in August of 1992, when you were interviewed, had you had any kind of training in acting? Had you done any kind of acting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have said in your various testimonies that the things you said on that tape were untrue. They were things that you made up and that you had good reason for doing that, and I'm not -- as I told you, not arguing with you about that. But just watching you during that interview, is there any way that we could know, just by watching you and listening to you, that you were telling an untruth, that you were talking about things that were not true? Is there any way we could know that without you telling us that? Just by looking at the way you were being interviewed? There isn't, is there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I'm not competent to assess these matters in such a way. I know what I said. I know what I had to say. And this is the third interview. During the first one, my attention was drawn to the fact that I have to say what had been written out for me. That was in the first interview. And that would probably safe my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is a very simple one. If, in 1992, 5th of May [sic], as had been suggested, any one of us was watching that programme on TV, listening to -- following your interview, would we have been able to know that you were lying during that interview, that you were saying what was -- what you knew was completely untrue? Or would we have had no reason to doubt what you were saying? This is the question that is being put to you. Any one watching you, would you have expected that person to have believed you or to have realised to understand that you were lying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to say in response to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 53, line -- it's actually page 54, line 1, I don't know if you said 5th of May but you clearly meant 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it should be corrected to show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing I want to ask you about that is just looking at you visually, this was four or five or six days, I take it, after you had suffered this severe beating that you told us about, being down on the floor, being kicked in the nose and the face, and being made completely bloody, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What medical treatment had you had following that severe beating?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No medical treatment was administered. The wound on the nose had healed because my skin had been scraped a bit, and I had a bad wound on the back. However, that healed too, a few months afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I think it was the very next day, after this interview, that you did on television, that Vojo Kupresanin came to Omarska and got you and took you with a police escort to Banja Luka, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Partly with a police escort, for part of the way. Most of the time we travelled without a police escort, for most of that journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The police escort would have been at the beginning of the journey as you were leaving Omarska and the Prijedor municipality, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not through the municipality of Prijedor. It was through Omarska and also for part of the journey through Banja Luka, but that was shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In the Stakic trial, page 4804 of the transcript, you told the Trial Chamber that when Kupresanin came and entered the room in which you were waiting, you thought he was someone else. Who was it you thought he was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that situation, at first glance, I had the impression that it was Mr. Slavko Bereta from the parliament, from the municipal assembly in Prijedor. That was my first impression at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After Mr. Kupresanin took you out of Omarska, you learned that there was some interest in you becoming a member of the parliament of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Kupresanin didn't tell me that. That's what I found out from a soldier who drove me to Vrbanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that was my question. You learned that there was some interest in you becoming a member of the parliament. And your answer is yes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that from the driver. So it wasn't official. It didn't come from one of the officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were told by Mr. Kupresanin that an agreement had been entered into with Fikret Abdic that Abdic would become the Prime Minister of the government of the Serbian Republic. You were told that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, so he told you that there was an agreement that Fikret Abdic would become the Prime Minister of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that it would be annexed to Bihac, that all of it would be one region, that they were negotiating to have Fikret Abdic Prime Minister of that government, and that a Serb should be president of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The whole idea of that happening and you being a member of the parliament and all of that was something that was rejected by you at least, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, Kupresanin never offered me to become a member of parliament. I heard from the driver, and I quote, "Good that you decided to be a member of the Serb assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course at that point you hadn't made that decision, had you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You hadn't decided to be a member of the Serb assembly, had you? You said the driver said it was good that you had made that decision. You had not made that decision, had you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course I hadn't, because I knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just for clarity of this particular transcript, could you tell the Judges who Fikret Abdic is and what role he played during that time, during the war?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war. That is a member of the Presidency of the collective body. Then he quit the Presidency, proclaimed a small area of Bosanska Krajina an autonomous region bordering on Croatia. Later on, he established military links with the Serbs seceded in Croatia and allegedly Serbs in Bosanska Krajina and which war against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the case isn't it that during the first multi-party elections that Fikret Abdic actually received more votes than Izetbegovic did. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And yet Izetbegovic was chosen as president over Abdic as President of the Presidency over Abdic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the Presidency session between the -- among the members of the Presidency. There was a kind of automatic reaction and the person who had won the most votes did not have to become automatically the President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to -- in speaking of the relative political positions of those two people, to say -- and I emphasise relative, to say that Izetbegovic was more of a Muslim extremist and Abdic more of a Muslim moderate?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Muslim extremists there, and in this regard, one could hardly spot any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's the case that Izetbegovic had actually been convicted and put in jail for espousing extremist Islamic views, hadn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was not the reason, but I'm not really familiar with this cases. It was a long time ago. And at that time I was not interested in that kind of topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Abdic was never put in jail for espousing extreme Muslim views, was he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Abdic did serve but for some other reasons, because of economic fraud, because he caused an economic collapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question. You are answering a completely different question, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Abdic was never put in jail for espousing extreme Muslim views, was he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in prison for other reason, for breaches of economic laws and for causing an economic collapse because he printed false bonds so that both of them had served their terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us about him forming his own autonomous province. He actually had a very large following among the Muslims there in the Bihac area, Velika Kladusa, that part of Bosnia, northwest Bosnia, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did. He organised it even in the military sense, he put together an army, and called it Autonomous Province of west Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And his people up there, as you suggested, actually engaged in fighting against the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in cooperation with the armed forces of Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cooperation with the armed forces of Serbs from Croatia, and allegedly, there was also some cooperation with the Army of Republika Srpska, but I wouldn't know much about that. That military cooperation mostly boiled down from what I heard from other people in procuring supplies and participation of the Serb brass, of Serb officers, in that Fikret Abdic's army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we are quite distant from the events of 1992 and early 1993 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that process, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During this process of being taken out of Omarska, taken to Banja Luka, spending time there, with Mr. Kupresanin and all the things you did there, you never encountered Mr. Brdjanin, did you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was clear to you, was it not, that Mr. Kupresanin, at apparently the urging of Mr. Karadzic was taking an interest in the camps and what was happening with the camps, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you what he said. I mean he made some inquiries about some people, about other non-Serb MPs from the area, and had some other plans in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at a document -- and I hope we can get through this real quickly -- look at a document DB111. Now, I think you've seen this document before, sir. And the question I want to ask you -- I have a couple of questions to ask you about it. The first thing you'll notice is that it has no dates filled in. It hasn't got a date of a session. The data session was held. It referred to it. It hasn't got a date, a decision date, where Dr. Stakic's name appears. It has no signature. It has no stamp. Doesn't it appear to you, sir, that what it is is a proposed decision that was never acted upon?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak only about my experience with documents, say in the parliament. I cannot say anything about this concrete document. I can also say the same thing that you said, that there is no date, no seal or anything, but sometimes such documents are made and prepared for large numbers of people attending various meetings, and it could only be the standard type of a document, but what is behind it, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I guess if -- with your experience in meeting in deliberative bodies, one of the things that might be the case with regard to this is it was a document that was prepared for a meeting of the War Presidency of Prijedor municipality, that it was presented to those attending that meeting, and not adopted and therefore no date was ever put on it. It was a proposal that wasn't accepted. Don't you think that's likely the case?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it were just a draft decision, I believe it would say that, because then you usually have it "draft" or "proposed document" or something and then it is only when one gets to the final document that it would say "decision." So I mentioned various possibilities that could be in play. I mean which one of them applies to this case, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the other thing that's -- that I find interesting in this document is that section headed, "Statement of reasons," and in that section it talks about the fact that there are no laws, either in the assembly of the Serbian Republic of BH are the Autonomous Region of Krajina that govern the seizure of property from citizens who participated in an armed rebellion and have left the territory. And neither are there any previous regulations applied in the Serbian Republic of BH, not in violation of the constitution that cover it. And it says, "Urgent passage of legislation that will govern this issue has been suggested in order for the proposed decision, that being this decision we are looking at, to have a legal foundation." It seems to me what they are saying there is even if this decision were adopted it would have no legal foundation, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read this last part, and I think it explains your dilemma. So there is a decision, but in order not to preserve the legal situation in which it is not justification, it is proposed to pass a law that would then ensure the legality of this decision. That is what I gather from what you read last but of course I cannot really speak about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think we agree. Okay. We are going somewhere else now. In the Keraterm case, it's the transcript of 28 May, 2001, at page 3957, Defence counsel, Mr. Greaves, asked you this question: "Did you approve of the fact that the SDA became an ethnically-based party?" And your answer was as follows -- and let me get it because I may not have it quoted exactly right. Let's make sure we are right. Your answer was as follows: "The SDA became predominantly national parties because the circumstances brought that about, because before that, another ethnic body, and that was the Serb, had organised the Serb people exclusively." Now, that wasn't -- that answer is not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which? Which part of the answer is not true, Mr. Ackerman, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, let me do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The part of that answer where you say the SDA became a national party because before that, another ethnic body, the Serbs, had organised the Serb people exclusively. Now, the proposition that before the SDA, the Serbs had organised a national party exclusively, is just not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fact is true. If we are talking about organisation. If we are talking about the date on which the party was registered, then you could say it was not true, because the SDA was registered with a court in Sarajevo sometime before the SDS but if we are talking about political -- about the political organisation, setting up of initial committees, then such organisation started amongst the members of the Serb people much earlier and across Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that dialogue that you had there with Mr. Greaves in that case on that day, you took the position that the SDA was not an ethnically based party, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, we did not want it to be one. We wanted it to be a party bringing together other ethnic groups as well, and we did score some initial success in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That party, that SDA party, was organised by Alija Izetbegovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group which included Alija Izetbegovic as the man who enjoyed the highest respect, who commanded the major -- the biggest authority in that group at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And isn't it the case that no reasonable person could view a party organised by Alija Izetbegovic as a multi-ethnic party?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you're right. In our Prijedor SDA, we even had two councilmen of different ethnicity, as SDA members. And I think that those two councilmen were sensible people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is an exhibit in our case, Mr. Sejmenovic, it's Exhibit DB1. It's in the form of a book written about the war in -- the name of it is, "The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." The authors are Berg and Shoup. I think it's not here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the book Mr. Donia had to testify upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, but we've never got a copy of it or any form of it whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman offered us a copy and we said we could buy our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it is going to be an exhibit we would like the Defence to give us a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is an exhibit I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, well in that case, can they please provide us with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll see if I can get another one. I hope it's not out of print. But I'll try to buy you one Ms. Korner not out of a huge sense of obligation but I would be happy to do that for you. We don't have it here but I don't think it matters, Your Honour. I have a page that I just want to quote some language from and ask him if he agrees with this language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a long quote, Mr. Ackerman or is it a short one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's all relative, Your Honour. I think it's short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if it's short perhaps we can have it photocopied or if you have a spare copy we could put it on the ELMO and everyone will be in a position to follow, at least to follow better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we put this on the ELMO, I can probably read it from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. The witness knows English as well so...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I cannot speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very well said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think his English has improved remarkably since the first time I met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because on his statement to the Prosecution, languages known, used, Bosnian and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, watching him write barn and garage today, I suddenly realised which I hadn't appreciated that his English clearly had improved but I think he's been learning English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll just read to you. There are two sections there that I've highlighted in yellow. "The Party of Democratic Action Stranka Demokratske Akcije SDA, was created in March, 1990, and led by Alija Izetbegovic. Izetbegovic had been an active proponent of expanding the role of Islam in public life and politics, although he carefully avoided specifically advocating the establishment of an Islamic state in Bosnia, the call for a greater role for Islam contained in his, "Islamic Declaration" of 1970 was widely interpreted as referring to Bosnia. It was for these views that he had twice been imprisoned under the communists. He represented a faction of the SDA inclined toward an identity defined largely in terms of Islam and intent on securing a dominant role for the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then the next section, "The overtly Islamic and Muslim nationalist orientation of the SDA leadership around Izetbegovic led to a split with the more secular Muslims within the party led by Adil Zulfikarpasic who formed his own Muslim party, the Muslim Bosniak Organisation, or MBO, in October 1990. This party held little appeal outside of liberal Muslim circles." Now, what these authors write there about the SDA and Izetbegovic and his views regarding the SDA is absolutely true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not absolutely. This is the impression that the writer gained. I disagree with it. I -- my opinion about all this is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's also true, isn't it, that -- that Izetbegovic's overt Islam Muslim nationalist orientation led to that split that caused the creation of the Muslim Bosniak Organisation? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a much more complex issue, and there are more reasons than only the ones that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's partly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can return the document to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm getting ready to embark on a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can break now for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Sejmenovic, we are going to go to Banja Luka now. After Kupresanin then had gotten you out of Omarska and brought to you Banja Luka you were taken to meet with Karadzic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the meetings was to be with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Where was that place that were you taken to meet with Karadzic? What building was that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building of the assembly in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there were several people there when you went there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you estimate the number, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot give you really a more specific number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At least among the ones you saw it was clear to you that it was a group of fairly -- fairly important people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that because of what Mr. Kupresanin said. He said, "You are going to meet president Karadzic now."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was end of August, beginning of September, wasn't it, somewhere in that range?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Among the people you saw there, you saw Srdjo Srdic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't know if the Judges know who he was. Tell the Judges who Srdjo Srdic was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was president of the SDS in Prijedor during the first term of office, and he was a MP in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later on a MP in the Serb assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at some point also the head of the Red Cross in the Prijedor area, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that he was a dentist. I am not aware of the fact that he was head of the Red Cross. Perhaps in the past but I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You saw Dr. Stakic there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who you didn't see there was Mr. Brdjanin. He was not there, was he, or you didn't see him at least?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You overheard Mr. Srdic complaining to people about Mr. Karadzic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And among the things he was complaining about was that Karadzic had given all power to municipal presidents, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was saying something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In early 1992, and I'm now going to a different subject but just very briefly, there was an economic blockade going on of the area in which you were situated, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which blockade you are referring to because all of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in certain types of blockade, economic that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were, in the Krajina area, there were really kind of two blockade problems. One of those being that because of the Croatian war, the regular supply of materials back and forth across the border to Zagreb and Croatia had been completely cut off, correct, so there was no commerce going on there at that point?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that direction. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the other -- the other issue had to do with what became known as the Posavina corridor. It was that corridor that was fought over that was blocking any commerce between the Krajina area and Serbia proper, correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That could be heard over the Serb media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I want to know is were you able to assess, just by observation, or whatever way, the effect of these various blockades, the lack of commerce from both Croatia and Serbia? What effect did that have on the Krajina region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not notice that because the area of Kozarac was already under blockade by the Prijedor army and police. People were not allowed to go to work, to school, and later on, even physical travelling was prohibited. So I cannot speak of any broader aspects because I did not really have any insight apart from news coming from the Serb media, in situations when I could hear these news or when I could hear interpretations thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's talk then about that period of time right at the beginning of 1992, before Kozarac was blocked off. Where you were able to go to Prijedor, you were able to move around. Did you see any effects of it at that point?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any major effects until then. What was noticeable was that there was a shortage of medicine and all of us together in Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to resolve it. As for other things that happened, I didn't know about that. From an economic point of view, perhaps there were some things. There were power cuts. That would happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you know, isn't it the case that certain factories had to dramatically reduce their work because there simply was no outlet for the product that they were producing? It could not be transported? Or in the alternative, they couldn't get the raw materials to produce the product? That happened, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened before that period too. At the moment when the changes took place in Slovenia and Croatia because most products from that area, that is to say from Bosnia-Herzegovina, were sold in that market or through that market, especially the export of raw materials. So this was felt by all towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina even before that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of a food shortage?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rumour had it that there were food shortages too but I'm not aware of any details. I just know from my very own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware, and you've testified about and we are going to another subject now, about the takeover of the transmitter at Mount Kozara, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I have another video clip that I want to play. I had asked the director to play it without sound but I think it should be played with sound so that Mr. Sejmenovic can at least hear what it's about. But I don't expect the translators to translate it. So we can just play it with normal sound and it starts at -- they know where it starts. It's at 3620 and I assume it's cued up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you see people in this tape that you recognise, would you say stop so that you can identify them for us?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. We see Mr. Srdjo Srdic here on the right-hand side wearing a white shirt. We can go on now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. On the left we see Mr. Kupresanin, and on the right is Mr. Srdic. We can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you stop please for just a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I may know him from sight, by sight. His face seems familiar but I couldn't know his name, no

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They just said that it was Andjelko Grahovac, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Grahovac was. I just say that the face seems familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead and play it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour I was just about to say. I don't think Mr. Ackerman made it clear but there is a full transcript of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm full aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He only wanted the witness to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in case Your Honours want to follow it, it's all in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact I was going to ask at some point in time because although Mr. Ackerman said that he's only interested in having the witness get the content of the -- of the words there, I think we ought to know too so I was going to ask in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour it's the continuation of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The full transcript Your Honours have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour's have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have not seen this tape before -- I hadn't seen this tape before so frankly, I don't know which transcript to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, you have. Sorry, do you remember yesterday it's the continuation tape of the interview with Mr. Sejmenovic so -- Your Honours were given a full transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a continuation of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suddenly realised Mr. Ackerman had not made that clear. All of this is transcribed into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner, for clarifying that. Mr. Ackerman do you have -- do you want the video to continue playing or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I want it to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's continue with the playing of the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead with the tape. Go ahead with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you stop, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that insignia that you see there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the interviewees already said that it was the wolves, some kind of wolves. I think that they came from the area of Croatia, from the police of the SAO Krajina, something like that. That's where insignia like this comes from, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the wolves of Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did hear about them and I think it was from the Serb media, as far back as the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about Milankovic from Prnjavor as being the leader of the Wolves of Vucjak?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall having heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We can continue with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour can I say that -- so that we've got an identification on the transcript, the P number was P1532 of the that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Slash, sorry, S151.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think it's the same number as the segment I played from the interview earlier too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope your question is not always the composer of the music.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I actually left those parts in because I thought you would enjoy the music, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a reason I wanted you to watch all of that, sir, and you're going to find out what it is here quite soon. What was going on there is they were celebrating the third anniversary of the takeover of that tower, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what they said, the people on this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these were people who were claiming some kind of a role in that process, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And all those people being interviewed, they were talking about three years ago, and how the transmitter was taken over and the process by which it was taken over and who the people involved were and things of that nature, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the answer, we are sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear your answer. I heard you say "da." Is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Throughout all those interviews and all the credits that people were being given for their efforts in that regard, not once did we hear the name Brdjanin, did we?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name was not mentioned a single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nor in all of the pictures we saw of the people that were there involved in that celebration did we see Mr. Brdjanin, did we?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not see him on this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you know, don't you, that that transmitter was taken over in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was sometime in mid-1992 or the beginning of the second half of 1991 rather.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I heard this in this particular video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess you were living in that area. You probably also noticed that the television changed in August of 1991, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Stakic, you were asked this question: "For the moment very briefly just the period before the takeover, did this assembly have any practical authority over events or bodies in the Prijedor region?" And the question really is not terribly related to the answer but what you said about halfway through your answer, and I'm on page 4481, was this: "The Autonomous Region of Krajina, at the moment of its founding, took over the military and television repeaters and installations on Mount Kozara and they interrupted the radio and TV programmes." That was not a true statement, was it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an accurate statement, according to what we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, isn't it the case that the transmitter was taken over before the Autonomous Region of Krajina was even created? The transmitter was taken over in -- at the latest, August of 1991 and the Autonomous Region of Krajina was not created until September of 1991. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that Krajina was in the offing, but we did not have any clear fact that Krajina had been founded. That is formally speaking, those MPs did not come forward and say, "We have set up Krajina." But in the parliament, during a session, or rather during an interval between the two sessions, I heard from Vojo Kupresanin, "We've made a region, taken the transmitter, and now we are airing our own programme." So that is how that was the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to look again at P12, please. You looked at this yesterday, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I want to you see it again because this is the 7th session of the assembly of the community of Bosnian Krajina municipalities held at 1700 hours on 16 September, 1991, and you will notice that right at the end of the paragraph -- the section denominated number 1, "after a vote, it was established that all deputies had voted unanimously to declare the Autonomous Region of Krajina." So that was the founding date of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally speaking, perhaps yes, but you've read it yourself that was the 7th session, and on the -- this tape, one of the protagonists said that the regional authorities were in the Europe restaurant and that they had taken a decision and explained why they were taking over the transmitter. You just saw it on the tape or as the speaker said, politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Bosnian Krajina municipalities, about the Autonomous Region of Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a matter of terminology. If you're asking me about it in the legal sense of the word, I do not know. I do not know because I had no access to these documents before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, but what you told the Trial Chamber in the Stakic trial was the Autonomous Region of Krajina at the moment of its founding took over these powers and transmitters and things?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what it means is that it already had taken the transmitter at the moment of their foundation, that at that time, they already had their tools of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On another matter, in your testimony -- let me find it -- it was 13 July, 1998, cause number IT-97-24-T, at page 612. You gave an answer to a question. You were asked about what is a Serb, basically, and you gave an answer that I thought was interesting and I want to ask you about it. What you said was, "For me, a Serb is a person that states openly that he or she is a Serb. We in Bosnia make this distinction among ethnic background very well. It's a matter of personal choice. There were people who were -- who were of a certain nationality but they stated that they were Yugoslavs and among Yugoslavs, the majority at least this is what the statistics showed, the majority of Yugoslavs were Bosniak Muslims." Now, the part of that answer that I'm interested in is where you said a Serb is a person who states openly that he or she is a Serb. And that we in Bosnia make these distinctions very well. It's a matter of personal choice. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when somebody says, "My ethnicity is Serb, Greek, Bosniak, Croat," then his ethnicity is the one that he has stated. I don't know what else could it mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if you were to decide tomorrow that you wanted to be a Serb, you could just announce that you're a Serb and you would be one? Is that what you're saying here?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the constitution and law, that is how it is, ethnicity is a matter to be decided freely by any citizen and nobody has the right to challenge it. Scientifically speaking, how these matters are treated is up to professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Historically, before 1974, in fact, it's the case that the Islamic people, the Muslim people, were not recognised as an ethnic group and many Muslims referred to themselves as Muslim-Serbs or Muslim-Croats, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the then communist law gave -- offered them only that possibility. In the previous period, they had no other possibility. They could only say they were Serbs or Croats. Later on, as undetermined. At the time that you're referring to, the communist authorities allowed them to declare themselves as Muslims and in no other way, or if they wanted to, as some other nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with that subject. We talked a little bit about the Kosarski Vjesnik yesterday, that Prijedor newspaper. It was a weekly paper, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if it was distributed anywhere outside Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a municipal organ, that is a newspaper of the municipality of Prijedor. Now, whether there were some copies sent to other towns, I do not know. Perhaps there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing it in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on sale?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, that it was really quite a local publication, published in limited quantity and very narrowly distributed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, that was a municipal newspaper, and most municipalities had papers of their own but that was an official organ, so possibly the municipalities were duty-bound to send individual copies to the archives in Sarajevo but I wouldn't be able to tell you anything more concrete about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm getting ready to go to a fairly long, new section. I would suggest that we break now and I have a matter that I would like to take up with you as soon as the witness leaves, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sejmenovic, we stop here for today, and we'll see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00, hoping that we will be in a position to conclude with your testimony tomorrow. You will be now escorted by the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing is to tell you that it's quite clear that I'm going to conclude fairly easily tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps as early as the end of the first break maybe a bit longer than that. I've moved pretty fast and skipped some material today so we are in good shape. The second thing, there was a -- I had made an inquiry about Sefer Halilovic material. The Prosecutor had extracted out some that they thought might fall within the category that I should have. It was given to the Court to look at and make a determination about and I'm wondering what's happened to. We haven't seen it back, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still have to discuss it with the other two Judges, and I hope to be able to do that by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, my legal assistants will try to identify that again so that we'll give it all due attention. Sometimes they fall by the way side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It happens with all of us, Your Honour. And the final thing is I will very soon certainly by next week, have completed all of my work with regard to the Rule 92 bis materials so that I can finish my answer to the Prosecutor's 92 bis thing, and also the Rule 94 part, although it was correct that I had all of those materials, what I didn't have was the names of the witnesses and I've now been furnished those and now I can go through those too and I think that will also be accomplished by next wee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only things changed for next week. With the change in dates, I think you now said that we were sitting on the 3rd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was told that there is no way you could bring anyone on the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we are still making inquiries but Your Honour, Lord Ashdown has asked that if he can now testify on the Friday rather than on the Wednesday because he has to be in business in Europe in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was going it testify on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct. Do I mean next week? Or the week after?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he will now be testifying on the Wednesday, the 4th instead of the 6th. I'm told and we are attempting to see whether the witness who Mr. Ackerman wanted out of the Rule 92 can be here instead on the Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thursday is a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thursday is a holiday and on the Tuesday we are trying to put back the one who was due on the Wednesday, so at the moment there are potentially three witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next week we are starting on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct, no, Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You told me that Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know but Your Honour you said we were going it sit Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's out of the question now because I delayed my return by one day knowing that you had no witnesses to produce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've also made plans the same way. We have people leaving town and not coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I asked because I could have returned Monday but when you told me that Tuesday you had no plans to bring forward witnesses, I said rather than travel long distance and odd hours on Monday, I will come back on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it perhaps -- it's now by the by but I understand that I think we said we would try. I didn't realise we a had given a blanket --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was given the indication that there was no use trying to sit on Tuesday because there was no possibility of -- Tuesday is the 3rd. Monday is the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right in that case, Your Honour, that solves that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to invite both of you to ensure that when Lord Ashdown comes here we will try and finish his testimony --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I put it this way, Your Honour? I don't think there is much chance that he's going to be staying on after that one session so come hell or high water, we are going to have to finish him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll meet tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.
